content: The studies reviewed included 23 trials, with 21 being cluster-randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and two being individual RCTs. Of these, 12 studies compared insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) to untreated nets, while 11 compared ITNs to no nets. Geographically, 12 studies were conducted in Africa (including Burkina Faso, Côte d’Ivoire, Cameroon, Gambia, Ghana, Kenya, Madagascar, Sierra Leone, and Tanzania), six in the Americas (Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Nicaragua, and Peru), four in South-East Asia (India, Myanmar, and Thailand), and one in the Eastern Mediterranean (Pakistan). Pyrethroid-only nets or curtains were shown to reduce all-cause child mortality compared to no nets or curtains, with high-certainty evidence. They also significantly reduced the incidence of uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria episodes and the prevalence of P. falciparum malaria, again supported by high-certainty evidence. Moderate-certainty evidence suggested that pyrethroid-only nets or curtains probably reduce the incidence of uncomplicated Plasmodium vivax malaria episodes, but they may have little to no effect on P. vivax prevalence, as indicated by low-certainty evidence. Additionally, pyrethroid-only nets or curtains reduced the incidence of severe malaria episodes compared to no nets or curtains. When comparing pyrethroid-only ITNs to untreated nets or curtains, moderate-certainty evidence suggested that they probably reduce all-cause child mortality. High-certainty evidence demonstrated that they reduce the incidence and prevalence of P. falciparum malaria. However, low-certainty evidence indicated that they may reduce the incidence of uncomplicated P. vivax malaria episodes, while the effect on P. vivax prevalence remains very uncertain. In areas with high insecticide resistance, ITNs treated with both piperonyl butoxide (PBO) and pyrethroid were found to reduce malaria parasite prevalence at 4–6 months of follow-up compared to pyrethroid-only ITNs, with high-certainty evidence. At 9–12 months and 16–18 months of follow-up, PBO-pyrethroid ITNs probably continued to reduce malaria prevalence, supported by moderate-certainty evidence. Similarly, at 21–25 months of follow-up, PBO-pyrethroid ITNs probably reduced malaria prevalence, although the evidence was of moderate certainty. Experimental hut trials in Africa demonstrated that unwashed pyrethroid-PBO ITNs resulted in lower mosquito blood-feeding success compared to unwashed pyrethroid-only ITNs. Similarly, washed pyrethroid-PBO ITNs reduced mosquito blood-feeding success compared to washed pyrethroid-only ITNs. In areas of high malaria transmission and pyrethroid resistance, trials comparing pyrethroid-chlorfenapyr ITNs to pyrethroid-only ITNs showed that the former reduced malaria prevalence. These trials were conducted in Benin and Tanzania. Additionally, pyrethroid-pyriproxyfen ITNs were compared to pyrethroid-only ITNs in three trials conducted in Benin, Burkina Faso, and Tanzania. These trials demonstrated that pyrethroid-pyriproxyfen ITNs may reduce malaria prevalence, although the evidence was of low certainty. Overall, the findings highlight the effectiveness of ITNs, particularly those treated with additional active ingredients like PBO, chlorfenapyr, or pyriproxyfen, in reducing malaria transmission and prevalence, especially in areas with high insecticide resistance.
